person.short: A Levite child saved from the river, raised as Pharaoh's daughter's son, who met God at the bush and led Israel to the edge of the promised land.

reign.text: Forty years, from the Exodus to the plains of Moab

verse.text: And when he was full forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brethren the children of Israel.
And when forty years were expired, there appeared to him in the wilderness of mount Sina an angel of the Lord in a flame of fire in a bush.
He brought them out, after that he had shewed wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, and in the Red sea, and in the wilderness forty years.

end.text: And Moses was an hundred and twenty years old when he died: his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated.

story.text: Moses was born in Egypt after Pharaoh had ordered that every son born should be cast into the river. His parents were Levites; later lists name them Amram and Jochebed, with Aaron and Miriam as his brother and sister. His mother hid him for three months, then laid him in a basket of bulrushes among the reeds while his sister watched. Pharaoh's daughter found him, and his sister fetched their mother, who was paid to nurse him. When the child grew, he became Pharaoh's daughter's son, and she named him Moses: "Because I drew him out of the water."

The book of Acts says Moses "was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians". When he was grown, forty years old by Acts' count, he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew and killed the Egyptian. The next day a Hebrew asked him, "Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?" Pharaoh heard of it and sought to kill him, and Moses fled to Midian. There he helped the seven daughters of the priest Reuel at a well, married one of them, Zipporah, and named their son Gershom: "I have been a stranger in a strange land."

Forty years later, Acts says, while he was keeping the flock of his father-in-law Jethro near Horeb, Moses saw a bush that burned but was not consumed. God spoke to him from it and sent him to bring Israel out of Egypt. Moses held back, saying he was "slow of speech", and God gave him Aaron to speak for him. On the road back to Egypt the LORD met Moses and sought to kill him, and Zipporah circumcised their son. Moses was eighty when he and Aaron stood before Pharaoh.

The forty years in which he led Israel out of Egypt and through the wilderness are told on his page as a leader. Exodus says that "the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend." When he came down from Sinai with the tablets, the skin of his face shone and he did not know it, and the people were afraid to come near him. When Israel made the golden calf, he broke the tablets, and then pleaded for the people, asking to be blotted out of God's book if they could not be forgiven.

Jethro brought Zipporah and her two sons, Gershom and Eliezer, to Moses in the wilderness at the mount of God. Later Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman he had married, and asked whether the LORD had spoken only by him. The text adds that "the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth." When Miriam was struck with leprosy, Moses cried, "Heal her now, O God, I beseech thee." Chronicles says his sons were counted with the tribe of Levi.

At Meribah, told to speak to the rock, Moses struck it twice with his rod, and God told him he would not bring the people into the land. Miriam died at Kadesh and Aaron on mount Hor. Moses begged to cross the Jordan and was told, "Let it suffice thee". From the top of Pisgah he saw the land, and he died in Moab at a hundred and twenty, "his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated"; no one knows where his grave is. Israel wept for him thirty days, and Matthew tells that Moses appeared with Elias, talking with Jesus on the mountain.

claim.text: His brother, three years older by Exodus 7:7, given to him as spokesman: "he shall be to thee instead of a mouth, and thou shalt be to him instead of God".
His sister and Aaron’s, "the prophetess", who led the women’s song at the sea and later spoke against him with Aaron.
"His servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, departed not out of the tabernacle"; he asked Moses to forbid Eldad and Medad.
The priest of Midian, his father-in-law, whose flock he kept when he was called at the bush.
Two men who prophesied in the camp; Moses would not forbid them.
With Dathan and Abiram he gathered against Moses and Aaron: "Ye take too much upon you".
Exodus does not name Pharaoh’s magicians, who did "in like manner with their enchantments". 2 Timothy names two men who "withstood Moses", Jannes and Jambres, and says no more about them.

Moses and Aaron brought Pharaoh the LORD’s word, "Let my people go", and Pharaoh answered, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go?" After the darkness Pharaoh told Moses he would die the day he saw his face again, and Moses answered, "Thou hast spoken well, I will see thy face again no more."

quote.text: Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Let my people go, that they may hold a feast unto me in the wilderness.

claim.text: Edom and Moab refused Israel passage, as Jephthah later recalled; he also asked of Balak king of Moab, "did he ever fight against them".
Both kings were defeated, and their lands given to the tribes east of the Jordan.

Moses went out from Pharaoh "in a great anger" after giving this word.
At the bush the LORD told Moses that the king of Egypt would not let Israel go, and that he would harden Pharaoh’s heart.
Exodus says again and again that Pharaoh’s heart was hardened "as the LORD had said"; once "as the LORD had spoken unto Moses", and once "as the LORD had spoken by Moses".

Deuteronomy says no prophet was like Moses "in all the signs and the wonders, which the LORD sent him to do in the land of Egypt"; Stephen speaks of "wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, and in the Red sea, and in the wilderness forty years".
On the night of the Passover the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt "by their armies", as he had commanded Moses and Aaron.

verse.text: And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea; and the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. And the children of Israel went into the midst of the sea upon the dry ground: and the waters were a wall unto them on their right hand, and on their left.

lines.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea and the LORD drove it back by a strong east wind; Israel crossed on dry ground and "believed the LORD, and his servant Moses".

more.text: After the sea, the people "believed the LORD, and his servant Moses".

He sang: the song at the sea, "Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD", and the song he spoke "in the ears of all the congregation" before his death. Revelation speaks of "the song of Moses the servant of God".
His sister and Aaron’s, "the prophetess", who led the women’s song at the sea and later spoke against him with Aaron.

verse.text: Behold, I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Horeb; and thou shalt smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it, that the people may drink. And Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel.

lines.text: Joshua fought Amalek while Moses held up his hands on the hill, with Aaron and Hur holding them steady; Moses built the altar "Jehovah-nissi".

more.text: At Horeb Moses struck the rock at the LORD’s word and water came out; at Meribah he struck the rock twice and the water "came out abundantly".
Moses judged the people alone from morning to evening; on Jethro's advice he chose able men as rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens, and kept only the hard cases.
Rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens judged the small matters; the hard cases came to Moses.

verse.text: And the LORD came down upon mount Sinai, on the top of the mount: and the LORD called Moses up to the top of the mount; and Moses went up.

lines.text: At Sinai Moses carried God's words to the people and theirs back to God; he wrote the words, read "the book of the covenant", and sprinkled "the blood of the covenant".

more.text: At Sinai the people asked Moses, "Speak thou with us, and we will hear: but let not God speak with us". Moses later said he "stood between the LORD and you at that time, to shew you the word of the LORD".
Exodus says "the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend", and Deuteronomy closes with a prophet "whom the LORD knew face to face".
Coming down with the tablets, Moses broke them, destroyed the calf, called "Who is on the LORD's side?", and then pleaded for the people: "blot me ... out of thy book".
Moses stood "in the breach" to turn God's wrath from the people.
Coming down from Sinai with the tables, Moses "wist not that the skin of his face shone", and the people were afraid to come near him.

verse.text: Then a cloud covered the tent of the congregation, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle.

lines.text: The tabernacle was set up on the first day of the second year, and the glory of the LORD filled it.

more.text: At the tabernacle the LORD promised to speak with Moses "from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims", and Numbers says Moses heard the voice there.
In the second year Moses and Aaron counted every man of twenty and over able to go to war.
Saying "I am not able to bear all this people alone", Moses gathered seventy elders; the LORD put of the spirit on Moses upon them, and they prophesied.
When Joshua asked him to forbid Eldad and Medad from prophesying in the camp, Moses refused.

When Aaron and Miriam asked whether the LORD had spoken only by Moses, the LORD answered that he makes himself known to a prophet "in a vision" and speaks to him "in a dream", but with Moses "mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches".

verse.text: And your children shall wander in the wilderness forty years, and bear your whoredoms, until your carcases be wasted in the wilderness.

lines.text: When the people refused to enter the land and spoke of choosing a captain back to Egypt, God sentenced that generation to forty years in the wilderness, all but Caleb and Joshua.

more.text: Against Moses' warning the people went up anyway; the Amalekites and Canaanites drove them back to Hormah.
Korah, Dathan and Abiram challenged Moses and Aaron: "Ye take too much upon you"; the ground opened and swallowed them.
"It came to pass, as he had made an end of speaking all these words, that the ground clave asunder that was under them".
Moses struck the rock twice and was told he would not bring the people into the land.
At Meribah Moses struck the rock and said "must we fetch you water"; God told him he would not bring the people into the land.
The Psalms say "it went ill with Moses for their sakes", because "he spake unadvisedly with his lips".
Aaron died on mount Hor in the fortieth year, and his garments passed to Eleazar.

At the LORD’s word Moses set a serpent of brass on a pole, and whoever was bitten and looked at it lived. Jesus said, "as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up".
When king Arad attacked, Israel vowed to destroy his cities and did so; the place was called Hormah.
Sihon refused passage and fought at Jahaz; Israel took his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok.
Og fought Israel at Edrei and was defeated, with his sons and people.
Moses sent a thousand from each tribe, with Phinehas, against Midian; five kings of Midian and Balaam were killed.
Moses gave the kingdoms of Sihon and Og to Gad, Reuben and half of Manasseh.
Moses asked Hobab the Midianite to stay as a guide: "thou mayest be to us instead of eyes".
The people often turned against Moses and Aaron: "Would God that we had died in the land of Egypt!"
A second census in the plains of Moab found none of the first generation alive except Caleb and Joshua.

verse.text: And Moses went up from the plains of Moab unto the mountain of Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, that is over against Jericho. And the LORD shewed him all the land of Gilead, unto Dan,

verse2.text: And the LORD said unto him, This is the land which I sware unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, saying, I will give it unto thy seed: I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither.

lines.text: Moses went up Nebo to the top of Pisgah, saw the land, and died in Moab.

more.text: In the fortieth year, after Sihon and Og, Moses began to declare the law beyond the Jordan.
Moses asked God to set a man over the congregation; he laid his hands on Joshua before Eleazar and all the people.
Moses wrote the law, gave it to the priests and elders, and had the Levites put the book beside the ark.
Before all Israel Moses told Joshua: "Be strong and of a good courage"; God gave Joshua the same charge at the tabernacle.
The LORD told Moses he would see the land but not enter it, because at Meribah "ye sanctified me not in the midst of the children of Israel".

"So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD." He was 120, "his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated"; "he buried him in a valley" over against Beth-peor, "but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day".
Jude says the archangel Michael "disputed about the body of Moses" with the devil.
At the transfiguration Moses and Elias appeared and talked with Jesus; Luke says they "spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem".
"There arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face."

tradition.text: Josephus, retelling Deuteronomy, says that as Moses was embracing Eleazar and Joshua "a cloud stood over him on the sudden, and he disappeared in a certain valley, although he wrote in the holy books that he died, which was done out of fear, lest they should venture to say that, because of his extraordinary virtue, he went to God."

Origen speaks of "the work entitled The Ascension of Moses (a little treatise, of which the Apostle Jude makes mention in his Epistle)", in which the archangel Michael disputes "with the devil regarding the body of Moses". The book is not part of Scripture.

burial.text: And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Beth-peor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day.

verse.text: And Moses and Aaron did so, as the LORD commanded; and he lifted up the rod, and smote the waters that were in the river, in the sight of Pharaoh, and in the sight of his servants; and all the waters that were in the river were turned to blood.
And Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt; and the frogs came up, and covered the land of Egypt.

And they did so; for Aaron stretched out his hand with his rod, and smote the dust of the earth, and it became lice in man, and in beast; all the dust of the land became lice throughout all the land of Egypt.

And the LORD did so; and there came a grievous swarm of flies into the house of Pharaoh, and into his servants’ houses, and into all the land of Egypt: the land was corrupted by reason of the swarm of flies.
Behold, the hand of the LORD is upon thy cattle which is in the field, upon the horses, upon the asses, upon the camels, upon the oxen, and upon the sheep: there shall be a very grievous murrain.
And they took ashes of the furnace, and stood before Pharaoh; and Moses sprinkled it up toward heaven; and it became a boil breaking forth with blains upon man, and upon beast.
And Moses stretched forth his rod toward heaven: and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and the fire ran along upon the ground; and the LORD rained hail upon the land of Egypt.
And Moses stretched forth his rod over the land of Egypt, and the LORD brought an east wind upon the land all that day, and all that night; and when it was morning, the east wind brought the locusts.
And Moses stretched forth his hand toward heaven; and there was a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days:

And it came to pass, that at midnight the LORD smote all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh that sat on his throne unto the firstborn of the captive that was in the dungeon; and all the firstborn of cattle.

reported.text: Daniel prays that "the curse is poured upon us, and the oath that is written in the law of Moses", and "As it is written in the law of Moses, all this evil is come upon us".

word.text: "The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me".

reported.text: In the temple Peter quotes the promise in his own wording ("him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you"; "every soul, which will not hear that prophet, shall be destroyed from among the people"), and a few verses on says, "Unto you first God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him to bless you". Stephen quotes it too: "This is that Moses, which said unto the children of Israel, A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear." Stephen does not say in that verse who the prophet is.

word.text: Moses wrote the law and gave it to the priests and the elders.

reported.text: Jesus said, "had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me", and after the resurrection that "all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me".

scriptureSays.text: Stephen calls him the man whom Israel refused as "a ruler and a judge", and whom God sent "to be a ruler and a deliverer".
"Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth."
God speaks with Moses "mouth to mouth", and calls him faithful "in all mine house".
"There arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face."
Moses stood "in the breach" to turn God's wrath from the people.
Later Scripture remembers the Exodus as led "by the hand of Moses and Aaron", with Miriam sent before the people too.

accession.text: Forty years before his call, a Hebrew had refused him: "Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?"
At Horeb, from the burning bush, God sent him: "I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people".
Moses said he was "slow of speech"; God gave him Aaron as spokesman: "thou shalt be to him instead of God".
Moses and Aaron gathered the elders; the people believed and worshipped.
He was eighty when he and Aaron spoke to Pharaoh.

claim.text: On the night of the Passover the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt "by their armies", as he had commanded Moses and Aaron.
After the sea, the people "believed the LORD, and his servant Moses".
Joshua fought Amalek while Moses held up his hands on the hill, with Aaron and Hur holding them steady; Moses built the altar "Jehovah-nissi".
Moses judged the people alone from morning to evening; on Jethro's advice he chose able men as rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens, and kept only the hard cases.
At Sinai Moses carried God's words to the people and theirs back to God; he wrote the words, read "the book of the covenant", and sprinkled "the blood of the covenant".
Coming down with the tablets, Moses broke them, destroyed the calf, called "Who is on the LORD's side?", and then pleaded for the people: "blot me ... out of thy book".
The tabernacle was set up on the first day of the second year, and the glory of the LORD filled it.
In the second year Moses and Aaron counted every man of twenty and over able to go to war.
Saying "I am not able to bear all this people alone", Moses gathered seventy elders; the LORD put of the spirit on Moses upon them, and they prophesied.

events.label: The spies and the forty years

claim.text: When the people refused to enter the land and spoke of choosing a captain back to Egypt, God sentenced that generation to forty years in the wilderness, all but Caleb and Joshua.
Against Moses' warning the people went up anyway; the Amalekites and Canaanites drove them back to Hormah.
Korah, Dathan and Abiram challenged Moses and Aaron: "Ye take too much upon you"; the ground opened and swallowed them.
Moses struck the rock twice and was told he would not bring the people into the land.
Aaron died on mount Hor in the fortieth year, and his garments passed to Eleazar.
When king Arad attacked, Israel vowed to destroy his cities and did so; the place was called Hormah.
Sihon refused passage and fought at Jahaz; Israel took his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok.
Og fought Israel at Edrei and was defeated, with his sons and people.
Moses sent a thousand from each tribe, with Phinehas, against Midian; five kings of Midian and Balaam were killed.

events.label: Land east of the Jordan given

claim.text: Moses gave the kingdoms of Sihon and Og to Gad, Reuben and half of Manasseh.
Moses asked God to set a man over the congregation; he laid his hands on Joshua before Eleazar and all the people.
In the fortieth year, after Sihon and Og, Moses began to declare the law beyond the Jordan.

events.label: The law written and handed over

claim.text: Moses wrote the law, gave it to the priests and elders, and had the Levites put the book beside the ark.
Before all Israel Moses told Joshua: "Be strong and of a good courage"; God gave Joshua the same charge at the tabernacle.
Moses went up Nebo to the top of Pisgah, saw the land, and died in Moab.

worship.text: The people answered "All the words which the LORD hath said will we do", and the covenant was sealed with blood.
They made a molten calf while Moses was on the mountain; about three thousand died that day.

building.text: Moses "finished the work" of the tabernacle, and the glory of the LORD filled it.

alliances.text: Moses asked Hobab the Midianite to stay as a guide: "thou mayest be to us instead of eyes".
Israel asked Sihon for passage along the king's highway; he refused and fought.

people.text: Rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens judged the small matters; the hard cases came to Moses.
A second census in the plains of Moab found none of the first generation alive except Caleb and Joshua.
The people often turned against Moses and Aaron: "Would God that we had died in the land of Egypt!"

claim.text: Moses was sent to Pharaoh to bring Israel out of Egypt.
Amalek fought Israel at Rephidim; the LORD swore war with Amalek "from generation to generation".
Edom and Moab refused Israel passage, as Jephthah later recalled; he also asked of Balak king of Moab, "did he ever fight against them".
Both kings were defeated, and their lands given to the tribes east of the Jordan.

rulers.name: Hur, one of five kings of Midian

claim.text: Five kings of Midian, Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur and Reba, were killed in the war of Numbers 31.

verdictNotes.text: At Meribah Moses struck the rock and said "must we fetch you water"; God told him he would not bring the people into the land.
The Psalms say "it went ill with Moses for their sakes", because "he spake unadvisedly with his lips".

dates.label: Scripture's own numbers
dates.note: Scripture gives Moses' ages (80 when he spoke to Pharaoh, 120 at his death) and forty years of leadership, but no year BC. The two dates below are scholars' reconstructions of the Exodus, not of Moses' life.

dates.label: Early Exodus (1 Kings 6:1 counted back)
dates.note: Mack (ISBE, 1915) counts the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 back from Solomon's temple and puts the Exodus about 1448 BC.

dates.label: Exodus under Merenptah
dates.note: Driver (1911) places the Exodus under Pharaoh Merenptah; these are that pharaoh's years on Petrie's dates, not the years of Moses' leadership.

outside.name: Manetho, as quoted by Josephus
outside.date: Quoted by Josephus, late 1st century AD; Manetho was an Egyptian priest-historian

claim.text: Josephus quotes the Egyptian writer Manetho as reporting that the lawgiver of a band of outcasts was a priest of Heliopolis named Osarsiph, who "was called Moses". Josephus rejects the story as fable. It is a hostile Egyptian tradition known only through Josephus, not a record from Moses' time.

twoAccounts.topic: How the judges under Moses were appointed

first.text: Exodus: Jethro sees Moses judging alone and advises him; Moses chooses able men and sets them over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens.

second.text: Deuteronomy: Moses tells the people "Take you wise men"; they agree, and he makes them heads. Jethro is not named.

death.text: Moses died in the land of Moab at 120 years old, "according to the word of the LORD", and Israel wept for him thirty days.

burial.text: And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Beth-peor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day.

scripture.text: The LORD told Moses he would see the land but not enter it, because at Meribah "ye sanctified me not in the midst of the children of Israel".

"So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD." He was 120, "his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated"; "he buried him in a valley" over against Beth-peor, "but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day".
Jude says the archangel Michael "disputed about the body of Moses" with the devil.
At the transfiguration Moses and Elias appeared and talked with Jesus; Luke says they "spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem".

tradition.text: Josephus, retelling Deuteronomy, says that as Moses was embracing Eleazar and Joshua "a cloud stood over him on the sudden, and he disappeared in a certain valley, although he wrote in the holy books that he died, which was done out of fear, lest they should venture to say that, because of his extraordinary virtue, he went to God."

Origen speaks of "the work entitled The Ascension of Moses (a little treatise, of which the Apostle Jude makes mention in his Epistle)", in which the archangel Michael disputes "with the devil regarding the body of Moses". The book is not part of Scripture.

questions.question: Are Jethro's judges (Exodus 18), the seventy elders (Numbers 11) and Moses' account in Deuteronomy 1 one event or more than one?

views.label: Two different bodies; Deuteronomy 1 retells Exodus 18

argument.text: Keil reads Deuteronomy 1:12–18 as Moses' own account of the Exodus 18 appointment, and the seventy elders as a separate council given the Spirit to help Moses govern.

views.label: One institution told in different sources
views.holders: Knobel and the critics from Vater onward, as reported by Keil

argument.text: These critics identified the seventy elders with the judges of Exodus 18 and took Deuteronomy 1:9–18 to refer to both, using the differences as evidence of separate documents. Keil reports and rejects this.

questions.question: Who "was king in Jeshurun" in Deuteronomy 33:5: Moses or the LORD?

argument.text: Henry takes the verse "rather" of Moses, who ruled the people after giving them the law, while noting that "some understand this of God himself".
Keil holds that "the subject in ver. 5 is not Moses but Jehovah", who became King in Israel at Sinai.

questions.question: Were the seventy elders the beginning of the later Sanhedrin?

views.label: Yes, a lasting council
views.holders: Talmudists, rabbis and many earlier theologians, as reported by Keil

argument.text: Keil reports the older view that the seventy formed a permanent body that lasted to the Captivity and was revived as the Sanhedrin.

views.label: No, a body for Moses' own time

argument.text: Keil holds that nothing more is recorded of the seventy, and that they did not form a permanent body.

questions.question: Were Eldad and Medad two of the seventy elders (Numbers 11:26)?

views.label: Yes, two of those chosen, who stayed in the camp
views.holders: Keil (1871 translation); Gray says this is how the verse "is generally understood"

argument.text: Keil calls them "two of the persons who had been chosen", who "had remained behind in the camp, for some reason that is not reported".

views.label: Of the wider body of elders, not of the seventy

argument.text: Gray points out that verse 24 says the seventy went out to the tabernacle and verse 25 that the seventy received the spirit, and that Moses' answer "implies that Eldad and Medad did not belong to the number". If the clause is original and not a later note, he says, it would be better to take "the registered" as "the whole body of elders from whom the seventy were chosen".

views.label: About the middle of the 15th century BC
views.holders: Edward Mack in the ISBE (1915), counting back by 1 Kings 6:1

argument.text: Mack counts the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 back from Solomon's temple and reaches "approximately 1448 BC", in Egypt's 18th dynasty.

views.label: In the 13th century BC, under Merenptah

argument.text: Driver argues from Exodus 1:11 that the oppression fell under Rameses II, who built Raamses and Pithom, so the Exodus came under his successor Merenptah.

questions.question: Who is the prophet "like unto me" of Deuteronomy 18:15–19?

views.label: The Messiah alone
views.holders: "The prevailing opinion in the early Church", revived by Kurtz, Auberlen and Tholuck, as reported by Keil (1871)

argument.text: Keil reports this as the early church’s main reading, which applied the promise directly and only to Christ, comparing Numbers 12:6–8, Deuteronomy 34:10 and Hebrews 3. Keil himself calls that use of those verses "unwarrantable".

views.label: The Old Testament prophets only
views.holders: von Hofmann, Baur and Knobel, as reported by Keil (1871)

argument.text: Keil reports that these scholars restrict the promise to the prophets of the Old Testament, "to the exclusion of the Messiah". He rejects the limit.

views.label: A line of prophets, with Christ included

argument.text: Both read "a prophet" as the prophets God would send whenever Israel needed a mediator, so that Israel need not turn to soothsayers. Keil adds that Christ, "in whom the prophetic character culminated", is included. Driver says the passage refers to "a prophetical order", and "may be reasonably understood as including" an ideal prophet in whom the line would culminate.

questions.question: Did Moses write the five books, and who wrote the account of his death?

views.label: Moses wrote them, apart from the last chapters

argument.text: Keil holds that "there is nothing in the whole of the five books which Moses might not have written", except "the last chapters of the fifth book", added "by a different hand" after Moses handed the finished book to the Levites (Deuteronomy 31:24). Of Deuteronomy 32:48–52 he says the account "was not written by Moses himself".

Driver concludes that Deuteronomy belongs "most probably, either to the reign of Manasseh, or to the early years of the reign of Josiah", in the 7th century BC, and that its author "builds upon the foundation of the prophets".

notSaid: Scripture gives no year BC for Moses or the Exodus, and never names the Pharaoh he faced.

Scripture gives Moses no fixed title for his office. It calls him "the servant of the LORD" and a prophet, and Stephen calls him "a ruler and a deliverer" (Deuteronomy 34:5, 34:10; Acts 7:35). Whether Deuteronomy 33:5 calls him king is disputed.
Moses' sons held no office of rule. They "were named of the tribe of Levi" (1 Chronicles 23:14-15), and the leadership passed to Joshua of Ephraim.
Nothing more is recorded of the seventy elders after Numbers 11.
Scripture names particular things Moses wrote (see "How the word came"), but the verses themselves do not say who wrote the five books as a whole.
Deuteronomy 34:6 says only "he buried him", and that "no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day".
John’s Gospel reports people asking about "that prophet" (John 1:21, 1:25; 6:14; 7:40), but does not cite Deuteronomy 18 at those places.
Exodus does not name the Pharaoh Moses faced, and Scripture gives no year BC for his call.

verse.text: And when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river’s brink.
Now when Pharaoh heard this thing, he sought to slay Moses. But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and dwelt in the land of Midian: and he sat down by a well.
Now Moses kept the flock of Jethro his father in law, the priest of Midian: and he led the flock to the backside of the desert, and came to the mountain of God, even to Horeb.
And Moses took his wife and his sons, and set them upon an ass, and he returned to the land of Egypt: and Moses took the rod of God in his hand.
And the children of Israel journeyed from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand on foot that were men, beside children.
And the children of Israel journeyed from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand on foot that were men, beside children.
And they took their journey from Succoth, and encamped in Etham, in the edge of the wilderness.
Speak unto the children of Israel, that they turn and encamp before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, over against Baal-zephon: before it shall ye encamp by the sea.
And when they came to Marah, they could not drink of the waters of Marah, for they were bitter: therefore the name of it was called Marah.
And they came to Elim, where were twelve wells of water, and threescore and ten palm trees: and they encamped there by the waters.

And all the congregation of the children of Israel journeyed from the wilderness of Sin, after their journeys, according to the commandment of the LORD, and pitched in Rephidim: and there was no water for the people to drink.
For they were departed from Rephidim, and were come to the desert of Sinai, and had pitched in the wilderness; and there Israel camped before the mount.

And they went and came to Moses, and to Aaron, and to all the congregation of the children of Israel, unto the wilderness of Paran, to Kadesh; and brought back word unto them, and unto all the congregation, and shewed them the fruit of the land.
This is the water of Meribah; because the children of Israel strove with the LORD, and he was sanctified in them.
And the children of Israel set forward, and pitched in the plains of Moab on this side Jordan by Jericho.
And Moses went up from the plains of Moab unto the mountain of Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, that is over against Jericho. And the LORD shewed him all the land of Gilead, unto Dan,
Pharaoh’s chariots and his host hath he cast into the sea: his chosen captains also are drowned in the Red sea.
